name: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease

criteria.description: Presence of multiple bilateral renal cysts detected by ultrasound or imaging, with number of cysts adjusted for patient age
Positive family history of ADPKD in a first-degree relative
Presence of extrarenal cysts (e.g., hepatic cysts) or intracranial aneurysms

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: At least two renal cysts in one kidney and at least two cysts in the contralateral kidney in individuals aged 30 years or older with a positive family history
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Imaging modalities include ultrasound, CT, or MRI. Genetic testing may support diagnosis but is not mandatory.

laboratory: Elevated serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen in advanced disease
Urinalysis showing hematuria and occasional proteinuria
imaging: Ultrasound showing multiple bilateral renal cysts
CT or MRI demonstrating renal and hepatic cysts
MR angiography for detection of intracranial aneurysms

distinguishingFeatures: Earlier onset in infancy or childhood
Enlarged echogenic kidneys without discrete cysts in early stages
Cysts predominantly in the medulla rather than cortex
Typically autosomal dominant but with different genetic mutations

redFlags: Sudden severe headache suggesting ruptured intracranial aneurysm
Gross hematuria with flank mass or severe pain
references: Torres VE, Harris PC, Pirson Y. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Lancet. 2007 Apr 14;369(9569):1287-301.
Cornec-Le Gall E, Audrézet MP, Rousseau A, et al. The PROPKD score: a new algorithm to predict renal survival in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2016 Mar;27(3):942-51.
Orphanet: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease - ORPHA:730
commonPitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as simple renal cysts, especially in younger patients with few cysts.
Confused with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) due to overlapping imaging findings in early childhood.
Hypertension and hematuria may be attributed to other causes, delaying diagnosis.
Liver cysts may be overlooked as unrelated findings rather than part of the disease spectrum.

extendedDiscriminators.feature: ADPKD typically presents in adulthood, whereas ARPKD presents in infancy or early childhood with enlarged echogenic kidneys.

ADPKD is characterized by bilateral, large, numerous renal cysts and often extrarenal cysts (e.g., liver), while medullary cystic kidney disease presents with small or normal-sized kidneys and no extrarenal cysts.
ADPKD shows multiple bilateral cysts with a positive family history, while simple cysts are usually solitary and sporadic.

ruleOutCriteria: Absence of renal cysts on imaging in an at-risk adult essentially excludes ADPKD.
Presence of only unilateral renal cysts without family history excludes ADPKD.
Genetic testing negative for PKD1 and PKD2 mutations in a patient with compatible imaging and family history makes ADPKD highly unlikely.
